items.content:
【Tianfeng Securities Overseas Technology】
Takeaways from an Interview with SanDisk IRD

1. Pricing remains a slightly larger contributor to FY27 Q1 earnings growth, but it is reasonable to estimate that pricing and volume each account for roughly half.

2. Volumes under long-term agreements are also fixed, with no room for adjustment. In many cases, volumes are specified not only annually but also quarterly or even monthly. Product types—including TLC/QLC and process nodes—are also explicitly stipulated.

3. HBF is not taking away HBM’s addressable market; it represents an additional memory tier. It is specifically designed for inference rather than training. In inference workloads, read operations significantly outnumber write operations.

4. YMTC is expected to capture an 80% share of the Chinese market. However, China’s market is growing so rapidly that even this would not be enough to satisfy demand. The impact of YMTC’s capacity expansion is material, but it is unlikely to become a major risk to global supply and demand over the next several years.

5. Asian investors are concerned about price declines in Q4 and Q1. However, the company has seen no signs of pricing deterioration to date and does not expect a material change in the 2027 supply-demand balance. The market remains tight. In fact, NBM customers are returning to request higher volumes or longer contract durations.

6. Finally, the company was asked, “What is the market’s biggest misconception about SanDisk?” The response remained extremely bullish. The market is still adjusting to a “new reality”—the sustainability of the business has fundamentally changed. Despite the company providing a range of supporting metrics, the market continues to question the sustainability of its business model.“The market is essentially telling you that the company’s terminal value is zero.”

items.content:
[Exclusive] SK hynix to Build Semiconductor Fab in Japan

SK hynix is moving forward with plans to invest tens of trillions of won to build a memory semiconductor fabrication plant (fab) in Miyagi Prefecture in northeastern Japan, according to sources familiar with the matter. If realized, it would mark the first large-scale investment by a South Korean semiconductor company to establish a local manufacturing base in Japan. However, as the Japan investment takes shape, U.S. pressure on Korean companies to expand memory production in the United States is also expected to intensify, further complicating their decisions over where to allocate future investment.

According to Hankyoreh’s reporting on the 20th, SK hynix is pursuing the construction of a memory semiconductor fab in Miyagi Prefecture, located in the Tohoku region of Honshu, Japan’s main island. A business community source said, “I understand that SK Group Chairman Chey Tae-won recently visited the area in person.” Miyagi is one of three regions, alongside Kyushu and Hokkaido, that the Japanese government is seeking to develop into major semiconductor industry hubs.

The investment is reportedly expected to amount to tens of trillions of won. Compared with the hundreds of trillions of won being invested in domestic semiconductor clusters in Yongin and the Honam region, the Japanese facility would represent a relatively smaller-scale production base. The Miyagi fab would be an additional overseas manufacturing site, while SK hynix proceeds with its planned domestic investments in the Yongin and Honam semiconductor clusters as originally intended. The move appears aimed at proactively expanding production capacity amid an ongoing global memory supply shortage.

If the plan materializes, SK hynix would become the third foreign semiconductor company, after U.S.-based Micron and Taiwan’s TSMC, to operate a semiconductor manufacturing facility in Japan. Samsung Electronics currently only operates an advanced semiconductor packaging research center in Yokohama.

However, the investment also carries risks. The United States has been pressuring the Korean government and Korean companies to invest in memory fabs on U.S. soil, and if SK hynix proceeds with its Japanese investment, Washington could intensify its demands for additional local production capacity in the United States. The company would also have to navigate domestic political uncertainty and public sensitivities in South Korea surrounding investment in Japan in a strategically important industry such as semiconductors.
— Jukan (@jukan05) Aug 20, 2026

items.title: "It could also position the company to respond proactively to the potential disruption that future memory disaggregation may pose to the traditional HBM business model." That’s how I see it too. SK hynix is preparing for a post-HBM era—a time when HBM may no longer be needed.
items.content:
"It could also position the company to respond proactively to the potential disruption that future memory disaggregation may pose to the traditional HBM business model."

That’s how I see it too. SK hynix is preparing for a post-HBM era—a time when HBM may no longer be needed.Jukan (@jukan05)【Tianfeng Securities Overseas Tech】 SK hynix CPO

At first glance, SK hynix’s CPO technology roadmap appears to have one axis pointing toward HBM and another toward optical communications. The underlying logic, however, is that AI competition is shifting from the performance of individual chips to the efficiency of data movement across the entire system.

Over the past several years, HBM has addressed the problem of GPUs not receiving data fast enough. Vertically stacking multiple layers of DRAM and placing them next to the GPU enables extremely high bandwidth. However, as more HBM stacks are placed around each GPU, packaging area, interposer-edge space, power delivery, and cooling are all approaching their limits. At the same time, AI clusters have already scaled to thousands or even tens of thousands of GPUs. No matter how fast each GPU can compute, the entire system will still hit the “bandwidth wall” if data cannot move efficiently between GPUs and racks.

SK hynix’s vision is to extend optical interconnects to memory. Low-latency, high-bandwidth local HBM would remain next to the GPU, while optical fiber would connect it to a larger shared memory pool. This would eliminate the need to fit all memory capacity within a single GPU package and enable horizontal scaling at the rack level.

The investment implications are as follows.

This does not mean that HBM will be replaced anytime soon. Instead, a new memory hierarchy is more likely to emerge. The most frequently accessed data would remain in local HBM, while larger volumes of less frequently accessed data would be stored in an optically interconnected memory pool, HBF, or SSDs.

SK hynix is repositioning itself. It is moving beyond selling standardized memory chips toward jointly designing HBM, controllers, advanced packaging, and system-level memory architectures with customers. If this roadmap materializes, SK hynix could strengthen customer stickiness, increase product value-added, and improve its ability to secure long-term contracts. It could also position the company to respond proactively to the potential disruption that future memory disaggregation may pose to the traditional HBM business model.

At the supply-chain level, areas likely to benefit over the long term include silicon photonics chips, optical engines, lasers, fiber coupling technologies, and advanced 2.5D and 3D packaging.

That said, this concept still appears to be at an extremely early stage—essentially just a roadmap. I interviewed someone involved in TSMC’s packaging operations today, and they were completely unaware of this initiative.—  https://x.com/jukan05/status/2090415402723791104 
— Jukan (@jukan05) Aug 20, 2026

items.content:
According to Taiwan-based media outlet DigiTimes, suppliers in Taiwan, Japan, South Korea, and China are expanding production capacity for higher-margin, advanced copper-clad laminates (CCLs) in response to supply shortages, but the capacity additions are running behind schedule.

Supply-chain sources cited by DigiTimes said Taiwan’s Elite Material Co. (EMC) and South Korea’s Doosan Corporation Electro-Materials BG have each seen their CCL equipment installation schedules delayed by about six months. Construction delays were cited as the cause at EMC, while Doosan’s delay followed a workplace safety incident at a construction site.

Taiwan Union Technology (TUC) has also experienced delays. Equipment delivery problems in the second quarter of 2026 pushed back mass production for the second phase of its Thailand plant by roughly two months. Nevertheless, production began in July, with shipments expected to increase from August as the plant ramps up.

These delays suggest that high-end CCL shortages and extended lead times are unlikely to ease in the near term.

Production capacity for AI server PCB-grade CCL remains concentrated among a small group of Tier 1 suppliers, including Taiwan’s EMC, TUC, and Nan Ya Plastics; Japan’s Panasonic Industry; South Korea’s Doosan; and China’s Shengyi Technology. With upstream material supplies also tight, lead times for high-end CCL have reportedly stretched to four to six months.

Supply-chain sources expect Doosan to be the sole supplier of CCL for compute boards during the initial production ramp of Nvidia’s Vera Rubin server platform. Meanwhile, Nan Ya is expected to join Shengyi and EMC in supplying materials for Vera Rubin switch boards.
— Jukan (@jukan05) Aug 20, 2026

items.content:
Samsung Electronics Accelerates Taylor Fab 2 Buildout, Asks Equipment Suppliers to Secure Certifications in Advance

Samsung Electronics is accelerating efforts to expand its advanced foundry capacity in the United States. Ahead of the planned groundbreaking for the second Taylor fab at the end of this year, the company has recently begun preemptively pursuing certifications required to introduce equipment from its suppliers.

According to industry sources on August 20, Samsung Electronics has asked key suppliers to obtain the certifications necessary to supply equipment for investment in the second Taylor foundry fab.

The Taylor facility will be dedicated to mass production using Samsung Electronics’ most advanced foundry technologies. Equipment is currently being moved into and installed at the first fab, which is scheduled to begin operations by the end of this year. Its primary production target is the industry-leading 2-nanometer process, with Tesla, a major U.S. technology company, widely cited as a key customer.

Samsung Electronics recently also formalized its plan to begin construction of the second Taylor fab. During its second-quarter earnings conference call on July 30, the company said, “To respond to growing customer demand in a timely manner, we are preparing to begin construction of the second Taylor fab by the end of this year, with mass production targeted for 2030.”

Samsung Electronics is believed to be demonstrating a strong commitment to investing in the second Taylor fab. The company has recently asked multiple semiconductor equipment suppliers to obtain “SEMI” certification in advance so their equipment can be installed at the facility. SEMI certification is a standard used to assess the safety of semiconductor equipment and must be secured before the equipment can be shipped overseas.

“Although the detailed specifications for the second Taylor fab have not yet been finalized, Samsung Electronics’ Foundry Business has begun responding more quickly than expected,” an official from the semiconductor equipment industry said. “Specific plans are expected to become clearer toward the end of this year, but the early action suggests that Samsung is actively preparing for the investment.”

The key issue is whether Samsung can secure major customers for its leading-edge processes. Samsung Electronics previously postponed its investment plans for the first Taylor fab several times due to difficulties securing customers during the initial phase of construction and a deterioration in market conditions. However, construction regained momentum after Tesla signed a KRW 22.76 trillion semiconductor contract-manufacturing agreement with Samsung Foundry in the third quarter of last year.

The roadmap for bringing the second Taylor fab into commercial production is likewise expected to depend on whether it is used to expand supply to Tesla or whether Samsung secures additional customers.

“I understand that Samsung E&A, Samsung’s engineering and construction affiliate, is also considering dispatching dozens of employees to the site to support construction of the second Taylor facility,” a semiconductor industry official said. “However, for Samsung Electronics to move swiftly from cleanroom construction to the installation of an actual mass-production line, it will first need to secure a major customer.”
— Jukan (@jukan05) Aug 20, 2026
